title: The judge that liked going first
scenario:
You lead e-commerce content at a home-goods retailer. An AI tool writes product descriptions. The team wrote a new prompt (B) and wants to know if it beats the current one (A).

A colleague set up a model judge and a small test. He says: "The judge picked A in run 1 and B in run 2. It's a tie, so let's keep A." The exhibit shows his notes.
exhibit:
Product descriptions: prompt A vs prompt B (made-up example data)

Judge: a model reads two descriptions side by side and picks the better one
Rubric: "Pick the better description."
Test set: 12 best-selling products, chosen by the marketing lead

Run 1  order A then B    judge picks A in 10 of 12
Run 2  order B then A    judge picks B in  9 of 12

Average length          A: 140 words    B: 95 words
Human editor, 12 pairs  prefers B in 8 of 12

Brand rules (from the style guide)
  - 100 words or fewer
  - must include the product code, e.g. "HG-2291"

Last quarter: 41 customer complaints about descriptions
  (wrong size, wrong material, missing care advice)

questions.prompt: What do runs 1 and 2 show about the judge?

options.text: The two prompts are equally good, so the team can safely keep prompt A.
options.explanation: The result flipped when only the order changed. That says more about the judge than about the prompts.

options.text: The judge works well, because it gave a clear winner in each of the two runs.
options.explanation: A clear winner that changes with the order is a warning sign, not a sign of a good judge.

options.text: The judge mostly picks whichever description it reads first: position bias.
options.explanation: Right. OpenAI's evaluation guide names position bias (response order) as a known problem with model judges.

options.text: The model is too small to judge text, so only human grading can work here.
options.explanation: The guides treat model judges as valid once they are calibrated. The fix is the judge setup, not dropping judges.

questions.prompt: What should happen before the team trusts this judge on thousands of descriptions?

options.text: Write a detailed rubric, control for length, and scale only once it agrees with human editors.
options.explanation: Right. OpenAI's guide says to use clear rubrics, control for length, and scale up only when the judge consistently agrees with human labels.

options.text: Run the same judge 10 more times in the A-then-B order and average the results.
options.explanation: Repeating the same biased setup repeats the bias. The order and the rubric are the problem.

options.text: Ask the judge to give longer explanations, so its choices look more convincing to the team.
options.explanation: Longer explanations don't fix the bias. Its choices still need to be checked against human editors.

options.text: Replace the judge with the human editor for every description, from now on.
options.explanation: Anthropic's guide calls human grading slow and expensive. Use people to calibrate the judge, not to replace it.

questions.prompt: How should the two brand rules be checked?

options.text: By the model judge, added to its rubric next to tone and style.
options.explanation: A judge can do it, but it is slower and less reliable than a simple rule for a clear-cut check.

options.text: By the human editor, who reads every description before it goes live.
options.explanation: Word counts and codes don't need human judgment. Save the editor's time for nuance.

options.text: By customers, who can report a wrong product code through the website.
options.explanation: That catches errors only after they reach customers. These rules can be checked before.

options.text: By a code check: count the words and look for the product code.
options.explanation: Right. Anthropic's guide calls code-based grading the fastest and most reliable method. It suits clear rules like these.

questions.prompt: What is the best change to the test set?

options.text: Keep the 12 best-sellers, because they matter most for revenue.
options.explanation: Twelve hand-picked easy cases miss the real failures. The complaints show where the tool breaks.

options.text: Build 20–50 tasks from the 41 complaints, each with a clear pass or fail rule.
options.explanation: Right. Anthropic's post says 20 to 50 simple tasks drawn from real failures is a great start, and two experts should agree on each verdict.

options.text: Ask the AI tool to write 1,000 test products, so that the set is large.
options.explanation: Generated tasks can help, but they don't replace the real failures you already have.

options.text: Remove the hard products from the set, so the scores look stable.
options.explanation: Hard and failed cases are what the test is for. Removing them hides the problems.
